An escaped dash is a literal class member, so the class is exactly {a, -, z}. Verified against bash 5.2 and glibc 2.36 fnmatch; awaiting confirmation from the next zlob 1.6.3 oracle run.

The escaped dash itself matches. zlob 1.6.3 treats the escaped dash as a range operator, so its verdict differs; bash 5.2/3.2, glibc 2.36 and BSD fnmatch keep it literal, which remains the primary expected result (issue #16).
The byte after the escaped dash is a literal member, not a range endpoint. Verified against bash 5.2 and glibc 2.36 fnmatch; awaiting confirmation from the next zlob 1.6.3 oracle run.

Regression for issue #16: the escaped dash used to open an a-z range. zlob 1.6.3 treats the escaped dash as a range operator, so its verdict differs; bash 5.2/3.2, glibc 2.36 and BSD fnmatch keep it literal, which remains the primary expected result (issue #16).

The backslash is consumed by the escape and is not itself a member. zlob 1.6.3 performs no escape processing inside classes and reads the backslash as a literal range start (0x5C-0x7A), so its verdict differs; bash 5.2/3.2, glibc 2.36 and BSD fnmatch keep the escaped dash literal, which remains the primary expected result (issue #16).

Without escape processing the backslash is a literal range start, so the class is {a} plus 0x5C-0x7A. Verified against glibc 2.36 fnmatch with FNM_NOESCAPE; awaiting confirmation from the next zlob 1.6.3 oracle run.

Without escape processing the dash is the range operator, so a literal dash is not a member. Verified against glibc 2.36 fnmatch with FNM_NOESCAPE; awaiting confirmation from the next zlob 1.6.3 oracle run.

An escaped byte may still start a range: the class is 0x2D-0x30. zlob 1.6.3 performs no escape processing inside classes and parses a reversed 0x5C-0x2D range plus literal 0, so the dash is not a member there; POSIX escape semantics remain the primary expected result (issue #16).
Upper endpoint of the 0x2D-0x30 range. Verified against bash 5.2 and glibc 2.36 fnmatch; awaiting confirmation from the next zlob 1.6.3 oracle run.

An escaped byte may still close a range: a-0x2D is reversed and therefore matches nothing. Verified against bash 5.2 and glibc 2.36 fnmatch; awaiting confirmation from the next zlob 1.6.3 oracle run.

The escaped dash is the reversed range endpoint, not a literal member. zlob 1.6.3 performs no escape processing inside classes and parses a reversed a-0x5C range plus a literal trailing dash, so the dash matches there; POSIX escape semantics remain the primary expected result (issue #16).
A trailing dash has no endpoint and stays literal. Verified against bash 5.2 and glibc 2.36 fnmatch; awaiting confirmation from the next zlob 1.6.3 oracle run.

A ] directly after the opening bracket is an ordinary member rather than the terminator.
That class holds nothing but the bracket itself.
Members written after a leading ] stay literal, and the class ends at the second ].
Negation applies to the leading ] member, so the bracket is the one byte excluded.
Everything outside that one-member set is accepted.
A caret negates the class the way ! does; POSIX leaves this unspecified and bash and glibc both accept it.
The negated member is rejected.
The leading caret is consumed as the negation marker and is not itself a member.
A caret anywhere but at the start is an ordinary member.
In the fnmatch reading a class may name the separator. The component-local matcher refuses it; see fast-glob.jsonl.
Ranges are byte ranges, so 0x2E to 0x72 contains the separator 0x2F. Found by the ferralk_vs_fast_glob differential target.

The leading-period rule outranks the class: no class may consume a period that starts a component. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; its own frozen Zig filesystem glob excludes it, as path-matcher.jsonl already records. ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
A range reaches the top of the byte space; matching is byte-first, not code-point-first.
The byte below the range is rejected.
Control bytes are ordinary class members.
A range whose endpoints are equal holds exactly one byte.
Nothing else falls inside a single-byte range.
Two POSIX class names may share one bracket.
A byte in neither named class is rejected.
A POSIX class name may sit beside an ordinary range in the same bracket.
A byte in neither the class nor the range is rejected.

An escaped ] is a member and does not close the class. zlob 1.6.3 performs no escape processing inside classes, so its verdict differs; POSIX escape semantics remain the primary expected result (issue #16).

The backslash is consumed by the escape, so it is not itself a member. zlob 1.6.3 performs no escape processing inside classes, so its verdict differs; POSIX escape semantics remain the primary expected result (issue #16).
An escaped ! at the start is a member, so this class is not negated.
Because the class is not negated, an unrelated byte is rejected.
